entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund (after eating) — never a finite clause. After the show ended is the conjunction, a different word class doing a different job. It does take the relative pronoun in after which (the vote, after which he resigned). After is also an adverb (we ate soon after) and an attributive adjective (the after party); the preposition always has an object.
entries.pattern: after [noun phrase] / after [verb-ing] / [measure phrase] after [noun phrase] / just, right, soon, shortly, or long after [noun phrase] / [clause], after which [clause]
entries.contrast: After is the plain word; following is its newsroom dress, subsequent to its legal one, post its finance-desk one, and none of the three is clearer. Against since: after names one later point, while since opens a stretch that runs up to now — after 2019 is any time later, since 2019 is the whole span. On the clock, after is the standard American word for minutes past the hour (ten after six) where British English says only ten past six.
entries.meaning: Places the main event later on the line than whatever follows after. It is the most general sequencing word in English and carries no meaning of its own beyond order — no cause, no consequence, no judgment about the size of the gap. 1. Later than a point in time. The pharmacy closes after nine. 2. Later than an event. After the surgery, she needed six weeks off. 3. Repeated succession, in the frame [noun] after [same noun]. day after day 4. Clock time: minutes past the hour (American). a quarter after three 5. In pursuit of, or in search of. The dog took off after a squirrel. 6. In imitation of, or in honor of. She was named after her grandmother. Senses 5 and 6 are not temporal at all, but they belong to the same word and appear constantly. Sense 6 is the American idiom; British English also says named for, which Americans use too but hear as slightly formal.
examples: The pharmacy closes after nine.
Call me any time after Tuesday.
After the surgery, she needed six weeks off.
He apologized only after being asked twice.
Day after day, the same gray sky.
One delay after another pushed the launch to March.
It was a quarter after three when the power came back.
The shuttle leaves at ten after the hour, every hour.
The dog took off after a squirrel and didn't come back for an hour.
Reporters have been after him for a comment all week.
She was named after her grandmother.
It's a courtyard after the Spanish style.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund (before leaving) — never a finite clause. Before you leave is the conjunction. Before is also an adverb with no object at all (I've seen this movie before), which is the surest test of the difference.
entries.pattern: before [noun phrase] / before [verb-ing] / [measure phrase] before [noun phrase] / just, shortly, or long before [noun phrase] / before long
entries.contrast: Before vs. by: before Friday excludes Friday, by Friday includes it — a deadline written with before is a day tighter than most writers intend. Before vs. ago: ago counts backward from now and takes the simple past (three days ago), before counts backward from a point already in the past and goes with the past perfect (he had left three days before). Before vs. prior to: identical in meaning, and before is a syllable shorter. Before vs. until: finish it before Friday is a deadline, wait until Friday is a duration.
entries.meaning: Places the main event earlier on the line than whatever follows before — the exact mirror of after. 1. Earlier than a point in time. We should be there before noon. 2. Earlier than an event. Sign the lease before the walk-through. 3. Earlier in an ordering or a queue, where the sequence is not literally temporal. B comes before C. 4. In the presence of a person or body with authority to judge. She testified before the committee. 5. Facing, or still ahead of, someone. The whole summer lay before them. Sense 4 is formal and mostly spatial — you appear before a judge, a court, a board, or a congregation — but it inherits the ordering logic of senses 1 through 3: the person judged comes first in line. Sense 5 is literary and always has a stretch of time or an opportunity as its subject.
examples: The mail usually comes before noon.
Get here before eight or you'll miss the opening.
Read the whole contract before signing anything.
Before the storm, nobody had bothered to trim the trees.
She quit two weeks before the merger was announced.
In the alphabet, B comes before C.
Your name comes before mine on the list.
Before long, the whole office knew.
He appeared before the zoning board three times.
The bill goes before the full Senate on Thursday.
At nineteen, she had the whole thing before her.

entries.complement: noun phrase — and, in older texts, a finite clause, where it is a conjunction instead (ere the sun set). A gerund is vanishingly rare and reads as pastiche; the period pattern is a bare noun phrase. No modern American writes any of it except for deliberate period effect.
entries.pattern: ere [noun phrase] / ere long / ere [the] [time noun]
entries.contrast: A dead-plain synonym of before, with nothing added but age. Do not confuse it with the homophone e'er (a contraction of ever), with err /ɜr/ ("to make a mistake"), or with air, which it is pronounced exactly like.
entries.meaning: Earlier than. You will meet it in hymns, in the King James Bible, in Shakespeare, in nineteenth-century verse, and in modern writing that is reaching for one of those. It survives in living American speech only in the fixed phrase ere long, and even that is bookish. 1. Earlier than a point in time. They were on the road ere dawn. 2. Earlier than an event. Not a word was spoken ere the reading of the will. 3. In the fixed adverbial ere long, before much time has passed. Ere long, the whole village had heard. Sense 3 is the only one a modern American is likely to write on purpose, and even it is a costume. Senses 1 and 2 are read, not written.
examples: They were on the road ere dawn.
He swore he would return ere nightfall.
Ere long, the whole village had heard.
Not a word was spoken ere the reading of the will.
Ere the year's end, three of them were dead.
Ere the last bell, the church was already full.
Ere the frost came, the last of the hay was in.

entries.complement: a noun phrase, characteristically one naming an event (following the announcement). A gerund is grammatical but clumsy, and a finite clause is impossible — there is no following the vote was counted. Note that the same string is also a present participle (the dog following me) and an adjective (the following week).
entries.pattern: Following [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] following [noun phrase] / immediately following [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: After means the same thing and is never ambiguous; following can be misread as the verb, which is why Following the mayor, the reporters filed out stalls a reader for half a second. Against subsequent to, following at least sounds like English. Reserve it for cases where the noun really is an event and after has already been used twice in the paragraph.
entries.meaning: After, in time, with a faint suggestion that the second event grew out of the first. 1. Later in time than a named event. Following the vote, the chairman resigned. 2. In the wake of, shading into cause. Three stores closed following the flood. That second sense is why press releases like it: following lets a writer imply a connection without claiming one. In careful prose that is a reason to distrust the word rather than a reason to use it.
examples: Following the vote, the chairman resigned.
A press conference is scheduled following the hearing.
Three stores on Main closed following the flood.
Following two years of losses, the company sold its warehouse.
The reception begins immediately following the ceremony.
Following his release, he moved to Tucson and said nothing more about it.
Following the recall, the company replaced its entire safety team.

entries.respell: in ad-VANSS uhv, weak in ad-VANSS uh
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in advance of filing) — never a finite clause. There is no in advance of he arrived; for a clause, use before. The bare adverbial in advance (pay in advance, a week in advance) takes no object at all and is the commoner form by far.
entries.pattern: in advance of [noun phrase] / in advance of [verb-ing] / In advance of [event], [clause] / [quantity of time] in advance (adverb, no object)
entries.contrast: In advance of is not a free synonym of before. It carries the idea of preparation — you do something early so as to be ready for what is coming. She trained in advance of the race is idiomatic because the training served the race; she was born in advance of the war is not, because birth prepares for nothing. Plain before has no such restriction, which is why it fits everywhere this phrase does and many places it does not. Against ahead of: the two overlap almost completely in the run-up sense, and ahead of is shorter. Against prior to: prior to is pure sequence with no preparation in it.
entries.meaning: Earlier than a coming event, and usually in preparation for it. The phrase is four syllables where before is two, so it earns its place only when the preparation is the point. 1. Early, in preparation for a coming event. Crews sandbagged the levee in advance of the storm. 2. In the run-up to a scheduled event, without the preparation sense. Both sides filed briefs in advance of the hearing. Sense 1 is the one that justifies the phrase. Sense 2 is the newsroom use, where it competes directly with ahead of and loses on length.
examples: Crews sandbagged the levee in advance of the storm.
Please submit your questions in advance of the meeting.
She trained for six months in advance of the race.
In advance of filing, the firm circulated a draft to the client.
Both sides filed briefs in advance of Tuesday's hearing.
The hotel needs a deposit two weeks in advance of your stay.
In advance of the audit, the department rebuilt its whole ledger.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ði ˈiv əv/, weak /ɑn ði ˈiv ə/
entries.respell: ahn thee EEV uhv, weak ahn thee EEV uh
entries.register: formal to journalistic — heavily used in news writing and history
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an event, and essentially nothing else (on the eve of the election, on the eve of war). No gerund — on the eve of signing is possible but stiff, and on the eve of the signing is the idiomatic repair. No finite clause. The article is fixed: on eve of is headline clipping, not prose.
entries.pattern: on the eve of [event noun] / On the eve of [event], [clause] / [clause] on the eve of [event]
entries.contrast: Literally it means the night or the day before, and in on the eve of Christmas it still does; figuratively it has loosened to mean "in the last stretch before," which can be a week or a year. That drift is why editors distrust it. Against ahead of and in advance of, both of which are neutral, on the eve of is the dramatic option — it exists to make the coming event sound momentous, so it wants a war, an election, a launch, or a verdict, not a dentist appointment.
entries.meaning: Immediately before a significant event, with the event's importance built into the phrase. The noun eve is a worn-down even, the old word for evening, which survives independently in Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve. 1. On the day or night immediately before, literally. They arrived on the eve of the wedding. 2. In the last stretch before a momentous event, figuratively. On the eve of the election, the polls tightened. Sense 2 has no fixed length and takes all the weight. If the event is not genuinely momentous, the phrase reads as inflation and before is the honest word.
examples: They arrived on the eve of the wedding.
On the eve of the election, the polls finally tightened.
The company announced layoffs on the eve of the holidays.
On the eve of war, the embassy burned its files.
He resigned on the eve of the vote he was certain to lose.
On the eve of the launch, a sensor failed and cost them the window.
On the eve of the trial, the state offered a plea.

entries.type: simple (a preposition clipped out of the Latin prefix post-)
entries.register: informal-to-neutral in business, finance, tech, and journalism; still rejected by conservative editors
entries.complement: a noun phrase, nearly always one naming an event or an era (post the merger, post pandemic). No gerund, no clause, and no article is required. It is far commoner as the hyphenated prefix (postwar, post-9/11, post-op), and that is the safe form in edited prose.
entries.pattern: post [event noun] / post [era noun] / post-[noun] as an attributive modifier
entries.contrast: It is after, in one syllable, borrowed out of a prefix. Against following and subsequent to — which are at least whole English words — post still reads as in-group jargon: post the acquisition is finance-speak for after the acquisition. The mirror form pre (pre the merger) exists but is rarer and sounds more British. When in doubt, hyphenate it onto a noun and it stops being controversial.
entries.meaning: After a named event or era. The usage grew out of postwar and post-Watergate, where the prefix was doing real work, and then broke free of the hyphen sometime in the late twentieth century. American editors split on it: it is unremarkable in an earnings call and conspicuous in a magazine. 1. After a specific event. Margins recovered post the merger. 2. After an era, usually with no article. Post pandemic, nobody wants five days in the office.
examples: Margins recovered post the merger.
Post pandemic, nobody wants five days a week in the office.
Head count is down twelve percent post the reorganization.
We'll revisit the forecast post earnings.
Post the recall, the stock never fully came back.
Everything in that neighborhood went up post-war.
Post the split, the two halves were worth more than the whole had been.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (prior to signing) — never a finite clause. For a clause you need before, since there is no prior to he arrived.
entries.pattern: prior to [noun phrase] / prior to [verb-ing] / [clause] prior to [noun phrase] / Prior to [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: It means before, exactly and only, in three syllables instead of two, and every American usage guide tells you to cut it. Keep it in contracts, protocols, and medical charts, where it is house style and where prior pairs with subsequent. Do not stretch it to mean in advance of in the sense of preparation — she trained in advance of the race is not she trained prior to the race.
entries.meaning: Earlier than. The phrase is built on the adjective prior ("earlier, previous"), which is why it attracts writers who want a sentence to sound procedural. In ordinary prose it adds length, not precision: prior to the meeting and before the meeting are the same statement. 1. Earlier than a stated event. All materials must be submitted prior to the deadline. 2. Earlier than a date or a year, as a background marker. Prior to 2018, the building had no sprinkler system. 3. Earlier than a stated action, with a gerund. Prior to signing, review the indemnification clause. Sense 3 is the one that carries real weight in drafting, because it attaches a requirement to an act rather than to a clock: prior to signing binds whoever signs, whenever that happens.
examples: All materials must be submitted prior to the deadline.
Prior to 2018, the building had no sprinkler system.
Patients should fast for eight hours prior to the procedure.
Prior to signing, review the indemnification clause.
He held two other posts prior to his appointment as chief.
Any defect reported prior to delivery is the seller's problem.
Prior to dispensing the medication, the pharmacist must verify the allergy list.

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a point in time (since Monday, since 2019, since the accident), a time adverb (since then, since yesterday), or a gerund (since leaving school). Never a length of time — since three years is the commonest single error in this file, and the word for a length is for. With a finite clause it is a conjunction (since I moved here), and with no object at all an adverb (I haven't seen her since).
entries.pattern: [perfect verb] ... since [point in time] / since [verb-ing] / ever since [point in time] / Since [point in time], [perfect clause] / since when (fixed)
entries.contrast: for / since / ago is the triangle: for takes a length (for three years), since takes a starting point (since 2022), and ago takes a length and counts backward from now (three years ago). Since also demands the perfect in the main clause — She has lived here since 2019, never she lives here since 2019. The causal since ("because") is the conjunction, not this word, and since meaning "afterward" (he has since retired) is an adverb.
entries.meaning: Opens a stretch of time that starts at a named point and runs up to the present moment. The "runs to now" part is built into the word, and it is why the main verb must be a perfect: the stretch is still open. 1. From a past point up to now. We've been waiting since eight. 2. From a past point up to some other past point, with the past perfect. By March he had not written since the funeral.
examples: We've been waiting since eight o'clock.
She's lived in Tucson since 2019.
Nothing has been the same since the fire.
He hasn't touched a piano since leaving school.
Ever since the surgery, he's walked with a cane.
By March, she had not heard from him since the funeral.
The building had stood empty since the previous tenant's bankruptcy.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause. There is no subsequent to he resigned; use after with a clause.
entries.pattern: subsequent to [noun phrase] / subsequent to [verb-ing] / [clause] subsequent to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The mirror of prior to, and heavier still: five syllables for a word of two. It exists mainly so that legal drafting can pair prior to with something symmetrical. Outside contracts and audit reports, write after.
entries.meaning: After. The adjective subsequent means "coming later," and the phrase inherits that and nothing more. It carries no implication of consequence, despite the family resemblance to consequent: subsequent to the audit says only that something happened later, not that the audit caused it. 1. After a stated event. Subsequent to the audit, three controls were rewritten. 2. After a date or a cutoff, in claims, warranties, and financial statements. Any claim arising subsequent to the closing date is the buyer's. 3. After a stated action, with a gerund. Subsequent to filing, the plaintiff amended the complaint twice. Sense 2 is the one with a technical life of its own: accountants call anything that happens after the balance-sheet date a subsequent event, and the phrase is the standard label for it. Senses 1 and 3 are ordinary after in a suit.
examples: Subsequent to the audit, three controls were rewritten.
Any claim arising subsequent to the closing date is the buyer's.
Subsequent to filing, the plaintiff amended the complaint twice.
The defect was discovered subsequent to delivery.
Subsequent to his resignation, the department was reorganized.
Two findings were disclosed subsequent to the balance-sheet date.
Subsequent to receiving notice, the tenant has ten days to cure.

entries.ipa: /əˈpɑn/, also /əˈpɔn/; first syllable already reduced to /ə/, so no further weak form
entries.register: formal — contracts, notices, and fixed phrases
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an event (upon arrival, upon receipt) or a gerund (upon signing, upon hearing the verdict) — never a finite clause. The gerund is the construction that keeps the word alive in modern American writing.
entries.pattern: upon [event noun] / upon [verb-ing] / Upon [noun phrase], [clause] / on or upon [receipt, arrival, completion, delivery]
entries.contrast: In the time sense upon means "at the moment of, and immediately after," compressing a whole clause: upon arrival is as soon as he arrived in two words. Plain on does the same job and is shorter (on arrival, on receipt); the two are interchangeable here and upon is the drafting choice. Against after, which allows any interval: after signing could be a week later, upon signing is that instant. The contact and movement senses live in upon.
entries.meaning: At the moment of the stated event, and therefore immediately after it. This is the one job in modern American English where upon is not merely a dressed-up on — it is the standard way contracts, invoices, and official notices attach an obligation to a triggering event. 1. At the moment a stated event occurs. Payment is due upon receipt. 2. With a gerund: as soon as someone does something. Upon signing, you have three days to cancel. 3. The frozen storytelling opener. Once upon a time...
examples: Payment is due upon receipt.
Upon arrival, please check in at the front desk.
The estate passes to her children upon her death.
Upon signing, you have three business days to cancel.
Upon hearing the verdict, he sat back down without a word.
The balance becomes payable upon completion of the work.
Once upon a time, this was all farmland.
Once upon a time there were three sawmills on this river.

entries.ipa: /ət ðə ˈtaɪm əv/, at weak /ət/, of weak /əv/ or /ə/
entries.respell: uht thuh TYME uhv, weak uht thuh TYME uh
entries.register: neutral to formal — legal, insurance, journalistic, and academic
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an event or a period (at the time of the accident), or a gerund (at the time of writing, at the time of filing) — never a finite clause. There is no at the time of he arrived; for a clause, use when. The frame at the time that [clause] is not an exception, since the clause there sits inside the noun phrase the time. The article is fixed in prose: bare at time of survives only as form-field clipping (at time of purchase, at time of service), which is why you meet it on receipts and nowhere else.
entries.pattern: at the time of [event noun] / at the time of [verb-ing] / At the time of [event], [clause] / at time of [purchase, service, sale] (fixed transactional clipping)
entries.contrast: Against during, which spreads an event across a whole period: an accident has no inside, so during the accident is odd where at the time of the accident pins a single moment. Against when, which is shorter but needs a subject and a tense — at the time of writing is the phrase's one indispensable use, because when I write this says something else. Against as of: as of this writing dates the claim from outside and is the commoner American business form; at the time of writing puts the writer inside the moment.
entries.meaning: Pins one event to the moment another event happened. It is the phrase that legal, insurance, and academic writing reach for when exact simultaneity is the thing at issue — a policy in force, an age, an address, a state of knowledge. 1. At the moment a stated event occurred. She was twenty-six at the time of the crash. 2. With a gerund, at the moment of doing something. At the time of writing, the bill had not been signed. 3. In the transactional frame, at the moment a transaction takes place. Payment is collected at the time of booking. Sense 3 is the one that drops its article on forms and signs. At time of purchase is standard on a receipt and wrong in a sentence; write at the time of purchase in prose.
examples: She was twenty-six at the time of the crash.
At the time of writing, the bill still had not been signed.
At the time of the merger, the company had nine hundred employees.
The policy had lapsed at the time of the fire.
Payment is collected at the time of booking, not at check-in.
He was living in Denver at the time of his father's death.
At the time of filing, neither party had counsel.

entries.complement: a noun phrase, or the paired frame between [X] and [Y] — the second half must be joined by and, never by or and never by to. Between 2 to 4 is always an error; write between 2 and 4 or from 2 to 4. Gerunds are fine in the paired frame — between finishing school and starting the job — and so is a bare plural or mass noun with no and at all (between meetings). No finite clause: between I got home and dinner is an error, and the repair is a noun phrase on each side. Pronouns take the objective case: between you and me, never between you and I. Between is also an adverb in in between (there's a week in between), where it has no object.
entries.pattern: between [time A] and [time B] / between [verb-ing] and [verb-ing] / between [plural noun phrase] / between now and [future time] / in between [noun phrase] / somewhere between [A] and [B]
entries.contrast: Between vs. among: the old rule that between is only for two is a myth — between is correct for any number of individually named points (between 1990, 1995, and 2000), and among is for an undifferentiated mass viewed collectively (among the war years). In time expressions among is almost never right. Between … and vs. from … to: from 2 to 4 is a run you occupy, between 2 and 4 is a window with slack in it — I'll call between 2 and 4 promises one call, not two hours of talking. Against within: between now and Friday names two edges, within two days measures one interval from now.
variants: betwixt (archaic and dialectal; alive only in betwixt and between)
'tween (poetic)
entries.meaning: Names the stretch that falls inside two stated edges, or in the gap that separates two recurring events. 1. A window bounded by two stated times. The pharmacy is closed between 1 and 2. 2. The interval separating two recurring events. She grades papers between classes. 3. The stretch from now to a stated future edge, in the fixed frame between now and [time]. We have three inspections between now and closing. Sense 2 needs a plural or a mass noun and no and: between meetings, between semesters, between jobs. It names the empty stretch that falls in the gaps, which is why between jobs is a polite way of saying unemployed. Sense 3 is the everyday planning frame, and it is the one place where between takes a single edge plus the present moment.
examples: The pharmacy is closed between one and two.
I'll call you sometime between Tuesday and Friday.
Between 1994 and 2001, the population doubled.
Between finishing school and starting the job, she spent a summer in Maine.
She grades papers between classes.
The house sat empty between tenants for most of that year.
He wrote three novels between teaching jobs.
There's a lot to do between now and Friday.
Two meetings ran long, and I ate lunch somewhere in between.
Between you and me, the deadline was never real.

entries.type: simple (historically the participle of the dead verb dure, "to last")
entries.complement: a noun phrase only — a noun naming a period or an event (during the war, during recess). Never a gerund (during eating is an error for while eating), never a finite clause (during I was there is an error for while I was there), and never a bare measurement of length (during three hours is an error for for three hours). Unlike most of the words in this file, during is only ever a preposition — no adverb, no particle, no conjunction — so it must always have a noun phrase after it and nothing else will do.
entries.pattern: during [the period or event] / During [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] during [noun phrase] / at some point during [period]
entries.contrast: during vs. for is the big one: during answers when and takes a named period, for answers how long and takes a measured length. It rained during the night (when) against it rained for six hours (how long). during vs. while: while takes a clause. during vs. throughout: throughout insists on the entire span with no gaps, during only says somewhere inside it, which is why he coughed during the concert does not mean he coughed for two hours.
entries.meaning: Locates an event inside a named stretch of time without saying where inside. 1. At some unspecified point within a period. The alarm went off during the meeting. 2. Across the whole of a period, when the verb or the context forces that reading. During the war she worked in a shipyard. Which sense you get is decided by the verb, not by during: a punctual verb (went off, called) gives sense 1, a durative one (worked, lived) gives sense 2. The preposition itself is neutral between them.
examples: The fire alarm went off during the meeting.
Somebody's phone rang twice during the second act.
During the war, she worked in a shipyard.
Nothing much grows here during the winter.
Please hold your questions during the presentation.
During my first year in Chicago, I didn't own a coat.
Three windows broke during the storm.
During the last two minutes, the arena never sat down.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈkɔrs əv/, of weak /əv/ or /ə/
entries.respell: in thuh KORSS uhv, weak in thuh KORSS uh
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a process or a stretch (in the course of the investigation), or a gerund (in the course of reviewing the file) — never a finite clause. The gerund is the whole reason to keep the phrase: during refuses one, so during reviewing the file is an error and in the course of reviewing the file is the repair.
entries.pattern: in the course of [process noun] / in the course of [verb-ing] / In the course of [noun phrase], [clause] / over the course of [measured span] / in the ordinary course of [business]
entries.contrast: In the course of and during both put something inside a stretch, and during is three syllables shorter — which is why usage guides call the longer phrase padding. It earns its place in exactly two spots: in front of a gerund, where during cannot go, and in in the course of employment, where a whole doctrine of workplace liability hangs on the words. Against over the course of: in prefers a process (in the course of the audit), over prefers a measured span (over the course of six months). Against throughout, which claims every moment of the span: in the course of claims only some moment in it.
variants: over the course of (the commoner form with a measured span — over the course of three years)
during the course of (redundant; editors cut the course of and leave during)
in the ordinary course and in the course of employment (fixed legal phrases that cannot be shortened)
entries.meaning: Somewhere inside a process or a stretch that is under way. The image is the older sense of course — a run, a path traveled — so the phrase suits things that unfold: an investigation, a career, a negotiation, an illness. 1. At some point inside a process already under way. In the course of the audit, two more accounts turned up. 2. With a gerund, while doing something. In the course of reviewing the file, she found the missing page. 3. Across a measured span, in the frame over the course of. Attendance doubled over the course of three seasons. Sense 3 is where the phrase is genuinely useful in ordinary prose: over the course of spreads a change out along a span in a way that bare over leaves flat. Sense 1 is the one to cut whenever during will do the same work.
examples: In the course of the investigation, two more accounts turned up.
In the course of reviewing the file, she found the missing page.
Nothing like it came up again in the course of his career.
The injury occurred in the course of employment, which is why the claim was paid.
Attendance doubled over the course of three seasons.
Over the course of six months, the debt was paid off entirely.
In the course of a single afternoon the whole plan fell apart.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈmɪdəl əv/, of weak /əv/ or /ə/
entries.respell: in thuh MID-ul uhv, fast in thuh MIDD-luh
entries.register: neutral to informal — the everyday spoken form
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period or an activity (in the middle of the night, in the middle of dinner) or a gerund (in the middle of eating, in the middle of moving) — never a finite clause. In the middle of I was eating is an error and the gerund is the repair. That gerund is what makes this the everyday spoken substitute for while, and it is the reason during eating has an idiomatic fix at all.
entries.pattern: in the middle of [period] / in the middle of [activity noun] / in the middle of [verb-ing] / right in the middle of [noun phrase] / be in the middle of [something]
entries.contrast: Against during, which takes a noun phrase and stops there: during dinner and in the middle of dinner both work, but only the second can carry on into a verb — in the middle of eating dinner. Against halfway through, which actually measures: halfway through the movie is a position on the clock, in the middle of the movie usually means only "while it was running, at a bad moment." Against at the time of, which is neutral: this phrase almost always brings interruption with it.
entries.meaning: Inside a period or an activity already under way, most often at the moment something cuts in. Literal centering is rare — in the middle of the night is any dark hour, not 12:00 sharp. 1. At some point inside a period, characteristically an inconvenient one. The phone rang in the middle of the night. 2. Inside an activity already under way, with a noun. He walked out in the middle of the ceremony. 3. With a gerund, in the act of doing something. I was in the middle of eating when they knocked. Sense 3 is the one worth drilling. During eating is an error and while eating is the textbook repair, but what Americans actually say is in the middle of eating — and unlike while, it needs no subject and no tense.
examples: The phone rang in the middle of the night.
He walked out in the middle of the ceremony.
We lost power right in the middle of dinner.
I was in the middle of eating when they knocked.
She's in the middle of moving and can't find anything.
In the middle of all this, the landlord raised the rent.
Don't call me in the middle of the workday unless something is on fire.

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period, nearly always with a modifier of extent in front of it (far into the night, well into his eighties, three weeks into the semester). After a measure phrase a gerund is idiomatic too — ten minutes into filming, two years into running the shop. No finite clause: into he arrived is not English. Note that into is only ever a preposition; it has no adverb or particle use, which is what separates it from bare in — come in is the adverb with no object, while come into the room still has one and is the preposition.
entries.pattern: [verb] into [the period] / far, well, deep, or late into [the period] / [measure phrase] into [period] / [measure phrase] into [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: in vs. into is the contrast to memorize here. In locates something inside a period; into adds motion, carrying the event across a boundary and onward — they talked in the night is a location, they talked into the night is a trespass past bedtime. Against through: through the night covers the night end to end, into the night only says the activity kept going past the point where it should have stopped. Against within: three weeks into the semester counts forward from the semester's start, within three weeks counts forward from now. The movement senses (into the room) live in into.
entries.meaning: Carries an activity across the edge of a period and keeps it going inside — or measures how far inside a period something happened. 1. Continuing past a boundary and on into a period. The argument went on into the night. 2. At a stated distance inside a period already under way. Ten minutes into the flight, an engine light came on. 3. Deep inside a long stretch or a stage of life, with well, far, or deep. She kept teaching well into her eighties. Sense 1 almost always carries a note of excess or persistence — you work into the night, not into the afternoon. Sense 2 is a measuring use and is perfectly neutral; it is the standard American way to time-stamp something inside an event, and it is why sportscasters say four minutes into the third quarter. Sense 3 needs its extent adverb: into his eighties alone is odd, well into his eighties is idiomatic.
examples: They argued into the night and settled nothing.
The renovation dragged on into a second winter.
The party ran late into Sunday morning.
Ten minutes into the flight, an engine light came on.
Three weeks into the semester, half the class had dropped.
Twenty minutes into filming, the generator quit.
Two years into running the shop, she still opens it herself.
She kept teaching well into her eighties.
The drought stretched far into the following spring.

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period (over the summer), an activity or a meal (over lunch), a medium (over the phone), a quantity of time (over an hour), or a condition being left behind (over the flu). No finite clause, and no gerund — over eating is not this preposition but the compound verb overeating, a different word. The one place a gerund turns up nearby is the frame over the course of writing it, where the gerund is the object of of and not of over at all. Over is also an adverb (it's over, come over), an adjective (the game is over), and a verb particle (think it over, the car flipped over); the preposition has an object and the adverb does not — compare the meeting is over with we talked it out over lunch.
entries.pattern: over [the period] / over the past / last [measured stretch] / over [meal, activity, or medium] / over [quantity of time] / over the course of [period] / be over [an illness or a feeling]
entries.contrast: Over vs. during: over prefers a span you survey from outside, especially a recent one (over the past decade), while during prefers a named event. Over vs. through: over the weekend surveys the span from outside, through the weekend runs it end to end without a gap. Over vs. for: over three hours means "more than," for three hours means "that long"; the opposite of that over is under (in under an hour). Over the weekend and on the weekend are standard American; British at the weekend is not.
entries.meaning: Spreads an event across a stretch of time that the speaker is looking at whole, from the outside. Every sense below is that same image applied to a different kind of stretch: a season, a measured run of years, a meal, a quantity, or an illness. 1. Across the whole of a named period, viewed as a span. We're driving to Duluth over the long weekend. 2. Across a measured stretch counted back from now, in the frame over the past / last [quantity]. Attendance fell over the last five years. 3. In the course of an activity, especially a meal, or by way of a medium. We settled it over coffee. 4. More than, with a quantity of time. The delay lasted over an hour. 5. Finished with, past the worst of — with an illness, a feeling, or a person. She's over the flu. Sense 3 is the one learners miss. Over dinner does not mean above the food; it means the conversation and the dinner occupied the same stretch, which is why over drinks, over lunch, and over the phone all work the same way. Sense 5 is the same reach-across image applied to a condition rather than a clock, and it is the sense that produces the flat American I'm over it.
examples: We're driving to Duluth over the long weekend.
The shop stays open over the holidays.
Enrollment dropped sharply over the last five years.
Over the past decade the neighborhood has turned completely.
They worked out the whole deal over coffee.
She told me over dinner that she was quitting.
We hashed it out over the phone instead of flying anybody in.
The outage lasted over an hour.
He's been with the company over twenty years.
She was over the flu by Thursday and back at work Friday.
He said he was over it, and for once he sounded like he meant it.

entries.complement: a noun phrase: a day, a date, a period, or the second element of a range. After a measure phrase it also takes a gerund — halfway through cooking dinner, partway through reading it. No finite clause: through the movie ended is not English. Through is also an adverb (let me through), a predicative adjective (I'm through with it), and a verb particle (see it through); the preposition takes an object and the adverb does not — compare we're through with we're through Friday.
entries.pattern: [start] through [end] / from [start] through [end] / all through [period] / through [period] / halfway or partway through [period or verb-ing] / get through [a hard stretch]
entries.contrast: This is the American inclusive-endpoint word, and it is one of the clearest AmE/BrE differences in the language. Monday through Friday includes Friday. British English writes Monday to Friday, which many Americans read as possibly stopping at the start of Friday. Against till and until, which stop at the boundary rather than including it: open until Friday is genuinely ambiguous, open through Friday is not. Against throughout, which claims the whole span emphatically and takes no range: there is no Monday throughout Friday. In contracts the belt-and-suspenders form is up to and including. The path senses (through the tunnel) live in through.
variants: thru (informal spelling — signs, notes, and menus only, never in prose)
entries.meaning: Runs an event along a stretch of time from one end to the other — and, in the American range use, includes the far end. 1. Up to and including the stated endpoint of a range. The office is open Monday through Friday. 2. From the beginning to the end of a period, with no gaps. He slept all through the movie. 3. At a measured distance inside an activity, with halfway, partway, or a fraction. We left halfway through the second act. 4. Out the far side of a hard stretch, usually with get, make it, or come. She got through the winter on savings. Sense 1 is the workhorse, and it is why American schedules, store hours, and government notices are less ambiguous than British ones. Sense 2 usually wants all in front of it and overlaps with throughout. Sense 4 always implies difficulty: you get through a winter, a diagnosis, or a divorce, not through a vacation.
examples: The clinic is open Monday through Friday.
Tickets are on sale through the end of March.
The exhibit runs June 3 through September 12.
Coverage lasts through December 31 and not a day longer.
He slept all through the second half.
She practiced through the whole summer without a break.
We kept the shop open through the holidays.
We left halfway through the second act.
Partway through cooking dinner, the power went out.
She got through the winter on savings and a lot of soup.

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period (or, in the spatial sense, a place). No gerund, no finite clause. It is also an adverb with no object at all (the mood stayed tense throughout), and that stranded use is common — the preposition has an object, the adverb ends the clause bare.
entries.pattern: throughout [the period] / Throughout [period], [clause] / [clause] throughout (adverb, no object)
entries.contrast: Throughout vs. during: throughout claims the entire span with no gaps, during is silent about coverage. He was quiet during the meeting allows him a sentence or two; he was quiet throughout the meeting does not. Throughout vs. all through: same meaning, and all through is the plainer, more spoken form.
entries.meaning: For the whole of a period, from one end to the other, without interruption. The word is emphatic by construction — through plus out — so it is wasted on short spans: throughout the afternoon is normal, throughout the minute is not. 1. For the whole of a period, with a state that holds without a break. It rained throughout the weekend. 2. At every point across a period, with events that keep recurring. Interruptions came throughout the hearing. 3. Everywhere inside a place — the spatial sense, listed here only so the split is visible. The company has offices throughout the Southwest. Senses 1 and 2 are the same claim of total coverage seen from two angles: sense 1 says a condition never lapsed, sense 2 says events kept coming and no stretch was spared. The verb picks the sense — a stative verb (rained, held, stayed) gives 1, a countable event (came, cried out, rang) gives 2. Sense 3 belongs with the place prepositions and has its own entry there.
examples: It rained throughout the weekend.
Throughout the 1970s, the plant ran three shifts.
She stayed calm throughout the entire ordeal.
Prices held steady throughout the year.
Throughout his presidency, the same three advisers kept their jobs.
The baby cried throughout the flight.
Interruptions came throughout the hearing, and the chair finally cleared the room.
The same warning is repeated throughout the manual.

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a length of time (within an hour) or a bounded period (within the fiscal year); also the frame within [length] of [event]. No gerund directly after within — but the of-frame takes one freely, since the gerund there is the object of of: within a week of moving in. No finite clause. In literary use within is also an adverb or a noun (a voice from within), where it has no object.
entries.pattern: within [length of time] / within [length] of [event] / within [the bounded period]
entries.contrast: in vs. within is the contrast worth memorizing. I'll be there in an hour means at the end of the hour — sixty minutes from now. I'll be there within an hour means at any point before the hour is up. For a deadline, within is the unambiguous word and in is not. Informal American also says inside of an hour for exactly the within meaning. Against by: by noon fixes a clock time, within two hours fixes an interval measured from now.
entries.meaning: Draws a boundary and puts the event inside it, before the far edge is reached. Everything within does is about a limit not crossed, which is why it is the deadline word of American contracts, warranties, statutes, and return policies. 1. Before a stated amount of time has elapsed. Reply within 48 hours. 2. Not more than a stated distance in time from some other event. She died within a week of her husband. 3. At some point inside a bounded named period. Within the fiscal year, the department has to spend it or lose it. Sense 2 works in both directions — within a week of the wedding can be the week before or the week after, and only context settles it. Sense 3 comes closest to plain in, and it survives as a separate sense only because a fiscal year, a term, or a legislative session has hard edges to be inside of.
examples: Please reply within forty-eight hours.
The package should arrive within three business days.
He was back on his feet within a month.
Cancel within thirty days and the fee is refunded in full.
She died within a week of her husband.
The lawsuit has to be filed within two years of the injury.
Within the fiscal year, the department has to spend it or lose it.
Within the first two weeks of the session, every bill has to be introduced.

entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (ahead of signing the deal) — never a finite clause. The fixed forms ahead of schedule and ahead of time take no article.
entries.pattern: ahead of [noun phrase] / ahead of [verb-ing] / ahead of schedule, ahead of time / Ahead of [event], [clause]
entries.contrast: Against plain before: ahead of adds either "earlier than the plan called for" (ahead of schedule) or the newsroom sense "in the run-up to" (ahead of Tuesday's vote), which has spread fast since about 2000 and which some editors still resist. Note that ahead of time is idiomatic and before time is not English. The opposite is behind.
entries.meaning: Earlier than a point that was already fixed. The word doing the work is already: there has to be a schedule, a due date, or a scheduled event for something to be ahead of, which is exactly the restriction plain before does not have. 1. Earlier than a scheduled or expected point. The bridge opened three months ahead of schedule. 2. In the period leading up to an event. Traders sold off ahead of the Fed announcement. Sense 1 is old and universal. Sense 2 is newer, is everywhere in journalism, and is the one to use sparingly: before the vote says the same thing without sounding like a wire report. The same newsroom slot is filled by on the eve of when the writer wants drama and by in advance of when the point is preparation.
examples: The bridge reopened three months ahead of schedule.
Pay the invoice ahead of the due date and you get two percent off.
Call me ahead of time if you're bringing anyone.
Traders sold off ahead of the Fed announcement.
Ahead of Tuesday's hearing, both sides filed briefs.
She resigned ahead of being formally charged.
Ahead of the holiday weekend, every flight out was already full.

entries.respell: AZ uhv, weak uhz uhv, uhz uh
entries.register: neutral to formal — business, legal, journalistic
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a date or a time point (as of Monday, as of this writing, as of yesterday's close). No gerund, no clause.
entries.pattern: As of [date], [clause] / [clause] as of [date] / as of [date], [figure]
entries.contrast: As of looks both directions, and that is its whole trick. Pointed forward it announces a change that takes force at that moment (as of July 1, the rate goes up); pointed backward it reports the state of things at that moment (as of Friday, 400 tickets were left). Effective can only do the first. Since opens a stretch; as of names its edge and says nothing about what follows.
variants: as from (British; Americans write as of or effective)
as at (British accounting, for a balance-sheet date)
entries.meaning: Names a date and pins a statement to it. Which way the sentence points — forward to a change or backward to a state — is decided by the tense of the verb, not by as of, and that is why the phrase can do both jobs with the same two words. 1. Starting from a stated date, looking forward. As of Monday, masks are optional. 2. Measured at a stated date, as a snapshot, looking backward. As of Friday, we had 412 registrations. The forward sense is an announcement; the backward sense is a reading off a meter. Sense 2 is why as of this writing and as of now are so useful — they date a claim without committing the writer to what happens next.
examples: As of Monday, masks are optional in the building.
As of January 1, the deposit goes up to two hundred dollars.
As of Friday, we had 412 registrations.
The account balance as of yesterday's close was negative.
As of this writing, no arrests have been made.
She is, as of last month, the longest-serving member of the board.
As of six o'clock, the roads through the pass were still closed.

entries.complement: in the temporal sense, a small and mostly fixed set of noun phrases — schedule, time, plan, or a competitor (behind the leader). Related but distinct is behind on + an obligation, where on is required and the object may be a noun or a gerund: behind on rent, behind on filing her taxes. No gerund directly after bare behind, and no finite clause. Behind is also an adverb (he stayed behind, we fell behind), a noun, and a place preposition; the preposition has an object and the adverb does not — compare we fell behind with we fell behind schedule.
entries.pattern: behind schedule / run, fall, or get behind [noun phrase] / behind [competitor] / behind on [obligation]
entries.contrast: The mirror of ahead of. Do not confuse the schedule sense with the place sense (behind the garage) or with behind the times, which means old-fashioned rather than late. Against past: past the deadline says the wall has been crossed, behind schedule says you are losing ground against a plan that is still running.
variants: behind time (chiefly British; American English says behind schedule)
entries.meaning: Puts something later than the standard it is being measured against — the mirror of ahead of. Like ahead of, it needs a plan, a clock, or a competitor for the lateness to be measured from; there is no behind in the abstract. 1. Later than a plan or a schedule required. The project is six weeks behind schedule. 2. Trailing a competitor at a given moment. He's a full lap behind the leader. 3. In the past and finished with, from the speaker's point of view. Those years are behind us now. Sense 3 always has the period as subject and a form of be — the worst is behind us — and it carries a note of relief that the neutral in the past does not.
examples: The project is running six weeks behind schedule.
We fell behind schedule the day the inspector showed up.
The train pulled in twenty minutes behind schedule. (British copy would say behind time.)
He's a full lap behind the leader.
Her fundraising is behind where it was at this point last cycle.
All of that is behind us now.
Two more weeks and the whole audit is behind us.
She's behind on rent for the second month in a row.
He's badly behind on filing his quarterly reports.

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a point in time or a limit; a gerund only in a closed set of idioms (beyond caring, beyond saving, beyond repairing). Never a clause. Beyond is also an adverb (the fields beyond) and a noun (the great beyond); the preposition has an object and the adverb does not — compare the years beyond with beyond the next two years. The spatial senses belong with the place prepositions.
entries.pattern: beyond [point in time] / beyond [a stated limit] / go, run, stretch, or extend beyond [time] / beyond [verb-ing] (closed set) / well beyond [time]
entries.contrast: Beyond midnight and past midnight both report a line crossed; beyond is the more literary of the two and is likelier when the crossing is unwelcome, surprising, or beyond anyone's plan. Against after, which is neutral about limits: the meeting ran beyond six says six was supposed to be the end, and the meeting ran after six is not idiomatic at all. Against over: over an hour counts a quantity, beyond an hour pushes past a stated ceiling.
entries.meaning: Puts an event on the far side of a limit, with the limit still in view. Where after names a later time and says nothing about it, beyond implies that the time it names was supposed to be an end. 1. Later than a stated time or limit. The talks went on beyond midnight. 2. Longer than a period was meant to last. Nothing on the schedule extends beyond Friday. 3. Past the point of, in a closed set of idioms. By then she was beyond caring. Sense 3 is the evaluative one and it is always about exhaustion or ruin: beyond help, beyond repair, beyond saving, beyond caring. It is the same reach-past-a-limit image as sense 1 applied to a condition instead of a clock.
examples: The talks went on beyond midnight.
Nothing on the schedule extends beyond Friday.
The lease runs beyond the end of the fiscal year.
He stayed at the paper well beyond retirement age.
Coverage does not continue beyond the warranty period.
By two in the morning she was beyond caring who won.
The car was beyond saving after the second winter.

entries.register: formal — contracts, procurement, military, official notices
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a point in time: a date, a clock time, or a named event (no later than close of business). No gerund, no finite clause. Not a length of time — no later than three hours is an error for within three hours.
entries.pattern: [obligation] no later than [point in time] / No later than [date], [clause] / NLT [date] (military and government shorthand)
entries.contrast: It is by with the ambiguity drafted out. By Friday leaves a reader wondering whether Friday itself counts; no later than Friday includes Friday and closes the question, which is exactly why contracts use the longer phrase. Against before, which excludes the stated day and is therefore a day tighter. Against within, which measures an interval from now rather than naming a fixed date.
variants: not later than (the older form, standard in statutes and regulations)
NLT (abbreviation, US military and federal usage)
no earlier than (the mirror form, which opens a window instead of closing one; a pair of them fixes both edges)
entries.meaning: The deadline phrase of American legal and administrative English. It names the last acceptable moment and includes it. Because it is explicit about inclusion, it is the safe form whenever the difference between two adjacent days has money or a right attached to it. 1. By a stated date or clock time, that date included. Proposals must be received no later than 5 p.m. on March 3. 2. By a point measured off another event. The tenant shall give notice no later than thirty days before the lease ends. Sense 2 is the drafting workhorse, and it is where learners slip: the measured phrase is still naming a point, not a length. No later than thirty days before closing picks a square on the calendar; no later than thirty days picks nothing and should be within thirty days.
examples: Proposals must be received no later than 5 p.m. on March 3.
The tenant shall give notice no later than thirty days before the lease ends.
Please submit the reimbursement form no later than the end of the quarter.
Report to the gate no later than forty minutes before departure.
No later than Friday, we need a decision from the board.
Payment is due not later than the fifteenth of each month.
Bids may be filed no earlier than March 1 and no later than March 15.

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a date, and essentially nothing else. No clock time in ordinary use, no gerund, no clause.
entries.pattern: on or about [date] / [clause] on or about [date] / On or about [date], [clause]
entries.contrast: It is about with a legal safety net. About June 3 hedges and leaves June 3 itself sounding excluded; on or about June 3 hedges while conceding that the exact day may have been June 3 after all. Pleaders use it so that a date proved to be off by a day does not defeat the allegation. In ordinary prose around June 3 says the same thing without sounding like a subpoena.
entries.meaning: On the stated date, or close enough to it that the difference does not matter legally. It is one of the few phrases in English whose entire purpose is to preserve a claim against an imprecise memory, and it is nearly invariable in American criminal charging documents. 1. On a stated past date, or near enough that the difference is immaterial — the pleading use. On or about June 3, the defendant deposited the check. 2. On a scheduled future date, allowing for slippage — the contract use. Delivery is scheduled to occur on or about the first of the month. Sense 1 protects an allegation from a witness's imperfect memory; sense 2 protects a promise from a carrier's imperfect logistics. Both are hedges, and neither belongs outside a legal document — in ordinary prose, write around.
examples: On or about June 3, the defendant deposited the check.
The parties entered into the agreement on or about January 15, 2019.
She was last seen on or about the evening of the fourteenth.
Delivery is scheduled to occur on or about the first of the month.
On or about that date, the account was closed and the funds withdrawn.
Closing shall occur on or about October 15, subject to the lender's schedule.
The complaint alleges that the calls began on or about the first week of April.

entries.ipa: /pæst/, no weak form of its own; in the fixed half past, fast speech clips it to /pəs/
entries.respell: PAST; half past six comes out haf-puss-six
entries.complement: a noun phrase — a clock hour, a time point, or a limit. A gerund appears only in a closed set of idioms (past caring, past praying for, past believing). No clause. Past is also an adverb (he drove past), an adjective (the past week), and a noun (the past); the preposition has an object.
entries.pattern: [minutes] past [the hour] / half past [hour] / past [time point] / past [a limit or a peak] / way or well past [time]
entries.contrast: On the clock, American English prefers after for minutes past the hour (ten after six) where British English uses only past — but half past and quarter past are alive and well in American speech, so past is no Briticism. British colloquial gone six ("just after six") has no American equivalent. Beware the homophone passed, which is the verb: we drove past the exit but we passed the exit. Against after: past midnight stresses that a boundary was crossed, after midnight just names a later time. The movement sense (drove past the house) lives in past.
entries.meaning: Puts a time on the far side of a line: the minute hand past a number, the clock past midnight, a thing past the end of its useful life. The line is always there in the meaning, which is what separates past from the flatly neutral after. 1. Minutes later than the stated hour. It's twenty past four. 2. Later than a stated time, with the sense of a line crossed. It was past midnight when they got in. 3. Beyond the limit of a period, a condition, or a capacity. He's past his prime. Sense 3 is where the word turns evaluative: past the deadline is a failure, past caring is exhaustion, past its expiration date is a warning. That judgment lives in past and not in after.
examples: It's twenty past four.
The meeting starts at half past nine.
It was past midnight when they finally got in.
The kids were up way past their bedtime.
The milk is a week past its expiration date.
He's past his prime as a starter, but he can still relieve.
By then she was past caring what anyone thought.

entries.complement: a noun phrase, characteristically one naming a decision or a process (pending approval, pending the outcome, pending trial, pending further review). No gerund, no clause. The same word is separately an adjective, both attributive (a pending lawsuit) and predicative (the case is pending); the predicative use is standard American.
entries.pattern: [clause], pending [noun phrase] / Pending [noun phrase], [clause] / held, suspended, frozen, or delayed pending [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Pending packs until and awaiting into one word: it names the event you are waiting for and marks the whole interval before it. Until takes a time point or a clause; pending takes the event itself, which is why pending approval works and until approval sounds clipped. It is not during: during the investigation covers the investigation, pending the investigation covers the wait for its result.
entries.meaning: While waiting for, and until, the stated event. The word was modeled on French pendant, "hanging," and that is exactly the image — the situation hangs in place until the awaited thing lands. 1. Until a stated decision or event occurs. He was suspended pending the outcome of the review. 2. Subject to, conditional on — a shading of the same sense. The sale is final, pending inspection. Sense 2 blurs into condition rather than time. If the emphasis is on the condition and not on the waiting, subject to is the more honest word.
examples: The officer was suspended pending the outcome of the review.
All hiring is frozen pending board approval.
He was held without bail pending trial.
Pending further instructions, the crew stayed on board.
The sale is final, pending a satisfactory inspection.
The grant is approved, pending a final head count.
Publication was delayed pending legal review.

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a point in time, or — as a conjunction — a finite clause (till the rain stops). Never a length of time: till three hours is an error for for three hours. No gerund.
entries.pattern: till [point in time] / from [time] till [time] / not ... till [point in time] / up till [point in time]
entries.contrast: Contrary to almost universal belief, till is not a shortened until — it is the older word by several centuries, and until was built out of it. Both are correct in American writing; till is a shade more spoken. The spelling 'til is the one with no historical footing, though it is everywhere, and untill is always a misspelling. For the meaning, see the by/until rule under until. In American clock time, till is also a regional word for minutes before the hour: a quarter till three.
variants: 'til (a back-formation from until; common but disliked by editors)
til (nonstandard)
until (the fuller and slightly more formal word)
entries.meaning: Up to a point in time, and then no further — identical in meaning to until. 1. Continuing up to a stated time. The bar is open till two. 2. Regional American clock time: minutes before the hour. ten till six Sense 2 is Midland and Southern American, alongside Northeastern of and general to. All three are standard American; only till in this use will strike a coastal ear as regional.
examples: The bar is open till two.
We waited till dark and then drove home.
He didn't say a word till the very end.
From Thanksgiving till New Year's, nothing gets done.
It's a quarter till three.
He gets off at ten till five.
Just hang on till Friday.

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a point in time, or — as a conjunction — a finite clause (until she calls). Never a length of time (until three hours is an error for for three hours) and never a gerund (until leaving is not English; write until he left).
entries.pattern: until [point in time] / from [time] until [time] / not ... until [point in time] / Until [point in time], [clause] / up until [point in time]
entries.contrast: by vs. until is the most useful contrast in this file. By is a deadline for a single completed action: Finish the report by Friday. Until marks a state or an activity that continues up to that point and then stops: Stay until Friday. The verb decides — punctual verbs (finish, submit, arrive, pay) take by; durative ones (wait, stay, keep, sleep) take until. Wait by Friday and finish until Friday are both broken. Against through: until Friday may or may not include Friday, through Friday certainly does.
variants: till (the older, slightly more spoken form)
up until and up till (emphatic)
'til (nonstandard but common)
entries.meaning: Marks the far end of a state or an activity that runs up to it and then stops. 1. Continuing up to a point in time, and stopping there. The store is open until nine. 2. In the not … until frame, the point at which something finally happens. He didn't call until Tuesday. 3. The whole stretch leading up to a turning point, in the emphatic up until. Up until the recount, she thought she'd won. Sense 2 is worth practicing, because the negative is doing real work: he didn't call until Tuesday says the call happened on Tuesday. Without the negative the sentence means something else entirely. Fronted for emphasis, the frame inverts: Not until Tuesday did he call. Sense 3 adds nothing to the meaning of sense 1 except emphasis on the length of the run-up, and up till is its more spoken twin.
examples: The store is open until nine on weeknights.
We stayed until the last song.
Until last year, the road was gravel.
The offer stands from now until the end of the month.
He didn't call until Tuesday.
Nothing was decided until well after midnight.
She didn't find out until the movers were already loading the truck.
Up until the recount, she thought she'd won.
Up until about 1990, every one of those storefronts was a hardware store.

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a time point (up to now, up to last Friday) or a quantity of time (up to six weeks). No clause. Note that up to + gerund belongs to a different idiom entirely (up to no good, what have you been up to), as does the "your decision" sense (it's up to you).
entries.pattern: up to [time point] / up to [quantity of time] / up to and including [date] / up to now, up to this point
entries.contrast: As a boundary, up to means until, but it is the natural choice with now and with measured quantities, where until cannot go: up to three hours is fine, until three hours is not. Against within: up to six weeks states a maximum, within six weeks promises a deadline. In contracts, up to and including settles the inclusive-endpoint question that ordinary American prose settles with through.
entries.meaning: Runs a stretch out to a stated edge and stops there — either the edge of a span already traveled or the ceiling on one still to come. Which of the two you get depends on whether the object is a point or a quantity. 1. Until a stated point, especially the present moment. Up to now, the plan has worked. 2. No more than — a stated maximum length. Delivery takes up to ten business days. 3. In the drafting phrase up to and including, out to a stated endpoint with that endpoint counted in. The lease runs up to and including December 31. Sense 2 is the one that ends up in advertising and warranties, and it is deliberately weak: up to 40% off promises nothing except a ceiling. Read it as an upper bound, never as an estimate. Sense 3 is what contracts write instead of trusting through, and it is the only form in this file that states inclusion in so many words.
examples: Up to now, the plan has worked.
Everything was fine up to last Friday.
Up to the very end he insisted the numbers were fine.
Delivery takes up to ten business days.
The battery holds a charge for up to eighteen hours.
The lease runs up to and including December 31.
Coverage continues up to and including the last day of the month.
Up to the day he retired, he opened the shop himself.

entries.complement: in this sense, a noun phrase naming a clock time, a date, or a quantity of time. No gerund and no finite clause in the time sense. (About + gerund exists — a book about running — but that is the topic sense, a different job for the same word, treated in about. About to + bare infinitive, as in about to leave, is a near-future construction and not a prepositional phrase at all.) About is also an adverb of degree (just about finished, about right) and, in older or regional use, an adverb of place (he wandered about); the preposition has an object and the adverb does not — compare we're about done with we're leaving about six.
entries.pattern: about [clock time] / at about [clock time] / about [quantity of time] / about [date or period] / about this time [last year, next week]
entries.contrast: About and around are freely interchangeable for time in American English. The mild tendency: around is a touch more casual and much commoner with holidays and seasons (around Christmas), about a touch commoner with measured amounts (about three weeks). Approximately is the formal register and belongs in lab reports, not conversation. British round about six is not American.
entries.meaning: 1. Approximately, with a clock time or a date. Come by about seven. 2. Approximately, with a measured stretch of time. It took about three weeks. Americans routinely stack at in front of it — at about six — which some style guides call redundant and which every American says anyway. It is standard spoken usage.
examples: Come by about seven.
The show starts at about eight thirty.
It took about three weeks to hear back.
She's been gone about an hour.
About this time last year, we were still in the old office.
The whole thing lasted about as long as a sitcom.
Give it about ten minutes and try the door again.

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a clock time, a date, a holiday, or a period. No gerund, no finite clause. The frame around the time [clause] is not an exception: the clause there is a relative clause inside the noun phrase the time, and around still has a noun phrase as its object. Around is also an adverb (she's been around, turn around) and a verb particle (hang around, stick around, come around); the preposition has an object and the adverb does not — compare he's not around with he got here around six. The spatial and movement senses (around the corner, around the lake) live in around.
entries.pattern: around [clock time] / around [date or holiday] / around [period] / right around [time] / around the time [that-clause inside the noun phrase]
entries.contrast: See about, with which it is interchangeable here. The thing to flag is the spelling: British writers use round where Americans must use around, and round about tea time is not an American sentence. Around is also the American choice in year-round, around the clock, and the other way around.
variants: 'round (informal American, as in 'round midnight)
round (the British form — in American English round is a noun, verb, or adjective, not this preposition)
entries.meaning: 1. Approximately, with a clock time. Let's say around six. 2. Approximately, with a date, a season, or a holiday. We'll be back around Labor Day. The holiday use is the one with no good substitute: around Christmas covers a fuzzy week or two in a way that on and at cannot, and about Christmas would be heard as the topic sense.
examples: Let's say around six.
He usually gets in around nine thirty.
We'll be back around Labor Day.
Around the holidays, nothing ships on time.
She moved to Denver around 2015.
The rent went up right around the time the new owners took over.
Around midnight the power finally came back on.

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a year or a date, and nothing else. Never a clock time, never a gerund, never a clause, and — this is the error to avoid — never a quantity of time: circa three weeks is wrong for about three weeks.
entries.pattern: circa [year] / c. [year] / circa [decade] / circa-[year] [noun] (hyphenated modifier)
entries.contrast: About and around work with any time expression; circa is licensed only for dating, and using it for durations marks a writer as reaching. In loose journalistic use it has spread to mean "in the era of" (circa-1975 Springsteen), which is a stylistic flourish rather than the dating word, and it is usually hyphenated when it modifies a noun that way.
variants: abbreviated c. or ca. before a year (c. 1450, ca. 1920); c. is the commoner American abbreviation
entries.meaning: Approximately, before a date whose exact value is unknown or disputed. It is the standard notation of museum labels, catalog entries, genealogy, and academic history, and its point is honesty: circa 1450 says the object was dated by inference rather than by record. 1. Approximately, before a year or a date. A Flemish altarpiece, circa 1450. 2. Loosely, "in the era of," as a hyphenated modifier in front of a noun. He showed up in a circa-1975 leather jacket. Sense 1 is the real word and it belongs to scholarship. Sense 2 is journalistic drift — circa-1975 Springsteen is a period label, not a dating claim — and it is the only place the word gets hyphenated.
examples: A Flemish altarpiece, circa 1450.
The photograph was taken circa 1918.
He was born circa 1770 in what is now Vermont.
The manuscript dates from c. 900.
Circa 1890, the whole street was boarding houses.
The whole neighborhood went up circa the postwar boom.
He showed up in a circa-1975 leather jacket.

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a point in time, and above all the edge of a period in the frame near the end, the beginning, the close, or the middle of [period]. No gerund, no finite clause. The comparative and superlative still work as prepositions (nearer the holidays, nearest the deadline). Near is also an adjective (the near future, a near miss), an adverb (don't come near), and a verb (as the deadline neared); the preposition has an object and the adverb does not — compare the deadline is near with we finished near the deadline.
entries.pattern: near [time point] / near the end / beginning / close / middle of [period] / nearer [time] / nowhere near [quantity of time]
entries.contrast: Near vs. toward: near the end of the month is a static position on the calendar, toward the end of the month has drift in it — something is still moving. Near vs. about and around: those two hedge a stated time on both sides (around six covers 5:50 and 6:10), while near leans to just before, and it is much rarer with bare clock times — an American says around six, not near six, but near midnight is idiomatic because midnight is an edge. Note nowhere near, which is the emphatic negative of quantity (nowhere near an hour) and is much commoner in speech than the positive.
variants: near to (chiefly British in this sense; American English drops the to — near the end of the year, not near to the end of the year)
entries.meaning: Close to a point in time without reaching it, and most at home at the edges of a named period. The temporal use is the spatial one carried straight over: near the door and near the end of the year are the same relation on different maps. 1. Close to the edge of a period, in the near the end of frame. Sales pick up near the end of the month. 2. Close to a named moment, especially one that is itself a boundary. They finally left near midnight. 3. In nowhere near: far short of a stated quantity of time. The repair took nowhere near two weeks. Sense 1 is where the word earns its keep — American writing uses it constantly for the last stretch of a month, a quarter, a term, or a century. Sense 2 is narrower than learners expect: near wants a moment that already reads as a boundary (midnight, dawn, closing), which is why near three o'clock sounds off where around three does not.
examples: Sales pick up near the end of the month.
Near the close of the century the mills all shut down.
They finally left near midnight.
He was hired near the beginning of her second term.
It rains here only near the end of summer.
Nearer the holidays, the parking gets impossible.
The whole repair took nowhere near the two weeks they quoted.

entries.ipa: /naɪ/, no weak form; in nigh on the on reduces to /ən/
entries.complement: in living usage, nigh on(to) + a measured quantity of time (nigh on thirty years). The bare preposition meaning "near" (nigh the river) is archaic. No gerund, no clause. Nigh is also an adjective and an adverb (the end is nigh, well-nigh impossible), and those are the forms most Americans actually meet.
entries.pattern: nigh on [quantity of time] / nigh onto [quantity of time] / well-nigh [adjective]
entries.contrast: It means almost, and almost is the word to use unless you are deliberately reaching for a backcountry or a biblical tone. The everyday American equivalent for durations is going on — going on forty years. Do not confuse it with neigh (what a horse does) or nay (the old-fashioned "no"); all three sound alike.
variants: nigh on
nigh onto (the only forms in living American use)
entries.meaning: Nearly, before a stretch of time. In American English it survives almost entirely in nigh on, in speech that is either rural, elderly, or putting on a voice. As an adverb it is healthier: well-nigh impossible is still current in formal writing. 1. In nigh on or nigh onto: nearly, before a measured stretch of time. He's worked that farm nigh on forty years. 2. Near, before a point in time — the bare preposition, archaic outside deliberate pastiche. It was nigh midnight before the last of them left. Sense 2 is the original preposition and it is dead in ordinary American writing. What survives is sense 1, and it survives as a hedge on a quantity rather than as a time preposition proper — nigh on forty years is doing the work of almost, not of near.
examples: He's worked that farm nigh on forty years.
It's been nigh onto a decade since anybody lived there.
Nigh on two hundred people showed up.
The old bridge stood nigh on a century.
We waited nigh on an hour before anyone came out.
Nigh on three weeks passed before anybody answered.
It was nigh midnight before the last of them left.

entries.ipa: /tɔrd/ (itself the reduced form, so no further weak form), also careful /təˈwɔrd/
