entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a time of day or a period, very often in the frame toward the end, the middle, or the close of [period]. No gerund, no clause. The direction senses (toward the door) live in toward.
entries.pattern: toward [time of day] / toward the end, the middle, or the close of [period] / toward [period]
entries.contrast: Toward evening means as evening comes on and has not arrived; by evening means at or before it; around evening means approximately at it. The difference is that toward keeps the motion in the sentence — something is still approaching. Against near: near the end of the month is a static position in time, toward the end of the month implies drift.
variants: towards (the British preference — both spellings are correct English and mean exactly the same thing, but American English writes toward; recognize towards in British copy and do not reproduce it. Pick one and hold to it through a document.)
entries.meaning: Approaches a time without arriving at it. Where at pins a moment and around hedges one, toward keeps something in motion on the way there, and that motion is the whole of what it adds. 1. As a stated time approaches, without reaching it. Toward evening the wind died down. 2. In the later part of a period. Toward the end of the semester everyone gives up. The word imports its spatial meaning wholesale: just as toward the door does not mean you got there, toward midnight does not mean midnight arrived.
examples: Toward evening the wind finally died down.
Toward midnight the noise from the street let up.
Toward dawn the rain finally stopped.
Toward the end of the semester, everybody stops reading.
Sales pick up toward the middle of December.
He grew quieter toward the end of his life.
Toward the close of the fiscal year, every department starts spending.

entries.complement: it follows its object, and the object must be a measured length of time — three days ago, a moment ago, a long time ago. Never a point in time (Monday ago is not English), never a gerund, never a clause, and never in front of its object (ago three days is not English). It also requires the simple past in the clause it modifies: He left three days ago, never he has left three days ago.
entries.pattern: [quantity of time] ago / [quantity of time] ago, [past-tense clause] / long ago / how long ago / not long ago
entries.contrast: for / since / ago: for three years measures a stretch, since 2022 names a starting point, three years ago names a point by counting backward from now. ago vs. before: ago counts back from the moment of speaking and takes the simple past; before counts back from a point already in the past and takes the past perfect — he had left three days before. This is why ago cannot survive the tense shift of reported speech: she said she had quit three years earlier, not three years ago. ago vs. hence is the forward-backward pair.
variants: agone (archaic; found in older verse and in some rural speech)
entries.meaning: Locates a point in the past by measuring backward from the present moment. It is the commonest preposition in modern English that comes after its object, a leftover from the Old English past participle āgān, "gone by" — literally three days gone by. 1. Counting back from now to a past point. We moved here six years ago. 2. In vague measures, a general past. That was a long time ago.
examples: We moved here six years ago.
The package shipped two days ago.
She called about ten minutes ago.
That was a long time ago, and nobody remembers it the same way.
Long ago, this was all orchard.
How long ago did you two meet?
Not long ago you couldn't get a coffee on this block.

entries.type: marginal (a fossilized subjunctive of the verb come)
entries.register: informal — folksy and regional in flavor, but understood everywhere
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a future time point — a day, a month, a season, a holiday, or an age (come Monday, come spring, come her next birthday). Never a past time (come last Monday is not English), never a gerund, never a clause.
entries.pattern: Come [future time], [clause] / [clause] come [future time] / [subject] will be [age] come [time]
entries.contrast: It means when [X] comes or by the time [X] arrives, and it is warmer and more colloquial than either. Unlike by, it sets no deadline — come Monday announces what will be true then, not what must be done before then. Its one hard restriction is direction: come can only look forward.
entries.meaning: When the stated future time arrives. The construction is a leftover subjunctive — come Monday is [when] Monday come[s] — which is why it takes no -s and resists any tense marking at all. It gives a sentence a settled, almost prophetic tone, and it is at home in country lyrics, farm talk, and political prediction. 1. When a stated future day, month, or season arrives. Come Monday, everything changes. 2. By the time a stated future point arrives — with an age or a length of service. She'll be ninety come August. Sense 2 is where the construction is most alive in ordinary American speech. It is the standard way to state an age or a tenure that has not been reached yet, and nothing shorter does the job: she'll be ninety in August loses the sense of a milestone waiting on the calendar.
examples: Come Monday, everything changes.
She'll be ninety come August.
Come spring, the whole hillside turns yellow.
Come November, none of this will matter.
He'll have been at the paper thirty years come the fall.
Come Tuesday, the rates go back up.
It'll be forty years come December since the mill closed.

entries.type: marginal (an adjective pressed into prepositional service)
entries.complement: a date, or a time adverb standing in for one (effective January 1, effective immediately, effective at midnight, effective next Monday). No gerund, no clause. It introduces only the moment at which a rule, an appointment, or a change takes force; it is not a general-purpose time preposition.
entries.pattern: Effective [date], [clause] / [clause], effective [date] / effective immediately / effective with [the next billing cycle]
entries.contrast: Effective looks forward only: it names the moment something starts to have force. As of does that and can also look backward to report a state — as of Friday, we had 400 orders, which effective Friday could not say. Beginning and starting do the same job in plainer registers, and British as from is the equivalent Britishism.
entries.meaning: Taking force from the stated moment. The word is an adjective everywhere else in the language (an effective argument), and it earns a place in this dictionary because in official writing it takes a bare date as its object and sits exactly where a preposition sits — usually fronted, with a comma. 1. Taking force from a stated date. Effective January 1, the deposit increases to two hundred dollars. 2. Taking force from a moment named by an adverb or a cycle rather than a date. Effective immediately, all travel requires written approval. Sense 2 is why the word survives at all: effective immediately has no one-word substitute, because now is a description and this is an instrument. Note that the object may be a bare date with no preposition of its own (effective Monday), which is the clearest sign the word has stopped behaving like an adjective.
examples: Effective January 1, the deposit increases to two hundred dollars.
Effective immediately, all travel requires written approval.
She resigned from the board, effective at the end of the month.
The new rates are effective Monday.
Effective with the next billing cycle, paper statements cost two dollars.
The appointment is effective the first of the month.
Effective at midnight, the contract is void.

entries.complement: it follows its object, and the object must be a measured length of time (three days hence, a century hence). Never a point in time, never a gerund, never a clause, and nothing at all may follow it.
entries.pattern: [quantity of time] hence / [clause], [quantity of time] hence
entries.contrast: The forward-facing twin of ago: three days ago counts back from now, three days hence counts forward. Ordinary American English says three days from now and leaves hence to contracts, sermons, and speeches. Do not confuse it with the far commoner conjunctive adverb hence meaning "therefore" (the road was closed; hence the detour), which takes no time phrase and is a different word entirely, or with the archaic adverb of place (get thee hence).
entries.meaning: Counting forward from the present moment to a future point. It is one of the handful of English prepositions that follow their object — ago, hence, and notwithstanding are the everyday examples — and where ago is neutral, hence is a deliberate reach for gravity — which is why it survives mostly in legal drafting and in sentences about the judgment of history. 1. Counting forward from now by a measured stretch. The lease expires two years hence. 2. In vague or grand measures, a general future. What we build now will be judged a century hence. The split is the same one ago makes in the other direction: sense 1 is a real interval a reader could put on a calendar, sense 2 is rhetorical distance. Sense 2 is the commoner one in speeches, and it is the reason the word sounds like a peroration.
examples: The lease expires two years hence.
A decade hence, none of these arguments will matter.
The court will reconvene thirty days hence.
What we build now will be judged a century hence.
Six months hence, the pilot program comes up for review.
The vote is set for two weeks hence.
A generation hence, nobody will remember which side won.
